claims.text: Microsoft’s Recall feature became a privacy scandal in 2024 because it was initially designed as an AI "memory" tool that automatically screenshotted the user's screen every few seconds and stored this data locally [Source: ev-1].

Although Microsoft claimed the data would be encrypted, security researchers demonstrated that the screenshots were actually stored unencrypted (in plaintext) within a local SQLite database [Source: ev-1].

claims.text: This implementation flaw meant that sensitive information visible on the screen—such as passwords, health data, and private messages—was captured by default and could be accessed by any process running under the user account [Source: ev-1].

The feature’s value proposition of providing searchable local memory conflicted with privacy expectations because it acted as a default-on recorder for all on-screen activity without adequate security protections [Source: ev-1].

In response to these findings and inquiries from regulators such as the Irish Data Protection Commission, the UK Information Commissioner's Office, and the Washington State Attorney General, Microsoft delayed the launch in June 2024 and subsequently reversed its design approach [Source: ev-1].
The changed version of Recall is now opt-in (default OFF) rather than enabled by default [Source: ev-1].
Additionally, accessing the timeline requires Windows Hello authentication and presence detection, and the feature explicitly excludes incognito browsing sessions and DRM content [Source: ev-1].
While this revised, more secure version reached general availability on Copilot+ PCs in 2025, the initial controversy permanently shaped privacy conversations surrounding AI PCs [Source: ev-1].
